standard.title: Tonal features and syllable representation
standard.description: recognise and use the tonal features of the target language in different contexts and understand how syllables are represented
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can recognise and distinguish tones, represent sounds in written phonetic form, and identify syllables in target language words (AC9LCH2U01). They can recite familiar rhymes and poems with attention to tone and rhythm. They have not yet used tones across different spoken contexts with developing accuracy, explained the romanisation or phonetic system as a learning tool, or investigated dialect diversity in the target language.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students recognise and use tonal features of the target language in different contexts with developing accuracy, understand how syllables are represented in the phonetic or romanisation system, and are aware of dialect diversity in the spoken language.

nodes.label: Tonal accuracy in speech
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can differentiate and produce the tones of the target language with increasing accuracy in speech, including in multi-syllable words and familiar sentences.
nodes.minimum_width: Produce all tones (including neutral tone where applicable) with recognisable accuracy in at least five words and demonstrate awareness of at least one tone change rule in context.
nodes.typical_width: Differentiate and produce the full tonal system in speech — including neutral tone and tone change patterns; use hand gestures or other physical cues to demonstrate tone; read aloud and recite familiar texts with attention to phrasing, stress and intonation.
wider: Record own speech and compare tonal accuracy with a model — identify specific tones that need attention and practise targeted improvement
Investigate how tonal errors change meaning in the target language — compile examples of minimal tonal pairs and discuss the communication consequences of tonal confusion
nodes.hinge_reason: Tonal accuracy is a prerequisite for intelligible spoken production in tonal languages. Students who cannot reliably produce the correct tone are producing words with different or no meaning — which undermines all subsequent spoken communication.

response_modes.reason: Tonal accuracy requires repeated production with feedback — not conceptual understanding alone. Regular reading aloud, recitation, self-recording and peer feedback activities build the muscle memory and perceptual accuracy that tone production requires.

success_criteria: Produces all tones with recognisable accuracy in at least five words
Demonstrates awareness of at least one tone change rule with a correct example

nodes.label: The phonetic or romanisation system as a learning tool
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain the purpose and use of the target language phonetic or romanisation system, and identify sounds that differ from their English equivalents.
nodes.minimum_width: Explain in simple terms what the phonetic or romanisation system represents and identify at least two sounds that appear similar to English letters but are pronounced differently.
nodes.typical_width: Explain that the phonetic system represents spoken sounds of the target language; match phonetic representations to syllables; identify sounds that differ from English equivalents; play matching games with phonetic forms; use the phonetic system as a reading and writing support tool.
wider: Analyse a section of target language text with phonetic annotation — identify where the phonetic form is most useful as a reading support and explain why
Investigate how the phonetic system handles sounds that do not exist in English — explain what these sounds are and how a learner could approach producing them

response_modes.reason: Understanding the phonetic system as a tool requires students to grasp the relationship between spoken sound, phonetic representation, and character — three distinct systems. Explicit instruction on how these relate, including common confusions between phonetic letters and English sounds, prevents systematic misreading.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Background learners who already know words orally often find the phonetic system revelatory — they can suddenly see the structure of what they have always said. Width investment here builds the metalinguistic bridge between oral knowledge and formal literacy in the target language.
success_criteria: Explains in simple terms what the phonetic or romanisation system represents
Identifies at least two sounds that differ from English equivalents and demonstrates the correct pronunciation

nodes.label: Dialect diversity in the spoken language
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify that the target language has dialect diversity and describe at least one example of phonological difference across dialects.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least two dialects or regional varieties of the target language and describe at least one way the spoken language differs across them.
nodes.typical_width: Investigate diversity in spoken varieties of the target language — dialects, regional accents, varieties spoken in different communities and countries; identify differences in phonology and compare with the standard form; appreciate the value of dialect diversity within the target language community.
wider: Research a specific dialect or regional variety spoken in the target language community — identify key phonological differences and where this variety is spoken

Compare the dialect spoken in the student's own family or community with the standard spoken form — identify specific differences and discuss their significance for the student's own language identity

response_modes.reason: Dialect awareness integrates tonal and phonological knowledge (nodes 1–2) with the broader social and cultural contexts in which the target language is spoken. The teaching investment is in creating space for students to recognise and value non-standard varieties — including those spoken at home — rather than treating them as errors.

success_criteria: Names at least two dialects or regional varieties of the target language
Describes at least one phonological difference across dialects with an example
